736.title: Wash in the Jordan (2 Kings 5)
736.hook: a proud general wants a grand cure, and his servant girl's advice gets him healed
736.howItsDone: Some Christians read Naaman's washing in the Jordan as a picture of humility and of grace that can't be earned, and some churches connect it with baptism, which in the Gospels also happens in the Jordan.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the mantle, and a student who refused to leave his teacher. Your line was I will not leave you. Which teacher did you reach out to? Day seven hundred thirty-six.

In the house of a great general, a young girl waits on his wife. She's from Israel, carried off in a raid. Her master is Naaman, captain of the army of the king of Syria, and the King James Bible sums him up in one breath: "a mighty man in valour, but he was a leper." Everything, and then that. One day the girl says to her mistress: "Would God my lord were with the prophet that is in Samaria! for he would recover him of his leprosy." A captive, wishing her captor well. And the mighty man listens. He sets off with a letter from his king, and silver, gold and changes of clothing. Today, wash in the Jordan.

Naaman pulls up at Elisha's door with his horses and his chariot. And Elisha doesn't even come out. He sends a messenger with one instruction: "Go and wash in Jordan seven times, and thy flesh shall come again to thee, and thou shalt be clean." Naaman is furious, and the text lets us hear exactly why: "Behold, I thought, He will surely come out to me, and stand, and call on the name of the LORD his God, and strike his hand over the place, and recover the leper." He had the whole scene planned: the prophet in person, a prayer, a hand waved over the place. Something worthy of a general. Instead: go take a bath. In a foreign river. "Are not Abana and Pharpar, rivers of Damascus, better than all the waters of Israel?" And he turns and goes away in a rage. Then his servants come near, and they say something wise: "My father, if the prophet had bid thee do some great thing, wouldest thou not have done it? how much rather then, when he saith to thee, Wash, and be clean?" If he'd asked for something hard, you'd have done it. This is easy. So Naaman goes down and dips himself in the Jordan seven times, "and his flesh came again like unto the flesh of a little child, and he was clean." Look at who carries his healing to him. A captive girl. A messenger at the door. His own servants. Every step comes through someone with no rank at all. And the cure itself is plain water, with nothing grand about it. The hard part was never the river. It was being willing to do something that small.
screen: `HEALED THROUGH THE ONES WITH NO RANK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find the plain thing. Settle, and breathe. Ask yourself what simple thing you've been putting off because it seems too small to matter, or too ordinary for the size of your problem. Making the doctor's appointment. Saying sorry. Answering the message you've left sitting. Asking for help. Notice if part of you is saying, like Naaman, behold, I thought it would be something bigger. Let that go by. Picture yourself doing the plain thing, once. If you pray, you can bring it before God. The bell holds the time.
Naaman. A proud general who wanted a grand cure, nearly walked away, and was healed by washing in the Jordan, on the word of people with no rank.
Your line: just wash. Today, do the plain thing you named, once, without waiting for it to feel important. Day seven hundred thirty-six.

737.title: Open his eyes (2 Kings 6:15–17)
737.hook: the servant sees enemy armies; Elisha prays and the hills are full of fire
737.howItsDone: Some Christians turn to Elisha's servant at Dothan in frightening seasons, and some pray Elisha's request, open his eyes, for someone who is afraid; the scene is also read in churches when teaching about angels and unseen help.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Naaman wanted a grand cure and got a muddy river. Your line was just wash. What simple thing did you finally do? Day seven hundred thirty-seven.

Early morning in a town called Dothan. A young man, the servant of the prophet Elisha, gets up before his master, opens the door, and steps outside. The hills around the town are covered. Horses. Chariots. A whole army from the king of Syria, sent overnight for one reason: to capture the man asleep inside. Elisha has been warning the king of Israel where the Syrians would lie in wait, not once nor twice, and the Syrian king has had enough. The servant runs back in, and the King James Bible keeps his words exactly as a frightened person says them: "Alas, my master! how shall we do?" Elisha's answer, and his prayer, are today.
screen: `ALAS, MY MASTER! HOW SHALL WE DO?`

segments.voice: Elisha doesn't say the army isn't there. It is. He says: "Fear not: for they that be with us are more than they that be with them." Hear how strange that is. Two men in a house, a cavalry outside, and he's counting, and his count comes out in their favor. Then he prays, and notice what he asks for. Not an escape. Not a fire from heaven. "LORD, I pray thee, open his eyes, that he may see." The prayer isn't for the situation to change. It's for the servant's sight to change. And it does. "The LORD opened the eyes of the young man; and he saw: and, behold, the mountain was full of horses and chariots of fire round about Elisha." The fire was already there. Nothing arrived. The young man just finally saw what had been standing on the hill the whole time. Then the story turns. The Syrians come down, Elisha prays again, and this time he asks for the opposite: that the soldiers be struck blind. He leads the whole confused army into the capital, Samaria, and when their eyes open there, the king of Israel wants to strike them down. Elisha says no. Set bread and water before them. So the king throws them a great feast and sends them home to their master. The chapter says the raiding bands of Syria came no more into the land of Israel. Christians have read this scene in more than one way. Some hear it about angels, a help that is real but usually unseen. Others hear it as a picture of faith itself: not seeing new things, but seeing the same hillside differently. Either way, the hinge is a three-word prayer for someone else.
screen: `THEY THAT BE WITH US ARE MORE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look for help you haven't counted. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind the thing that feels like an army on the hill right now. Let it be as big as it is. Then, slowly, start a second count. Who is on your side in this? A friend, a sister, a neighbor, a doctor, someone who prayed for you without saying so. What strength have you already got that you forgot to list? If you pray, you can borrow Elisha's words for someone else: open his eyes, or open her eyes. If you don't pray, just keep counting quietly. The bell holds the time.
Dothan. The town where Elisha's frightened servant saw the hills full of horses and chariots of fire, after a prayer: open his eyes.
Your line: more with us. Today, when something looks like it's surrounding you, stop once and count what's on your side, out loud if you can. Day seven hundred thirty-seven.

738.title: The lost book (2 Kings 22)
738.hook: workmen find the law in the temple, and young King Josiah tears his clothes
738.carry: the book was lost in the house
738.howItsDone: Some Christians mark a return to Bible reading by remembering Josiah's discovery, and churches sometimes use 2 Kings 22 to encourage people to read scripture for themselves and aloud together.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a frightened servant at Dothan, and the prayer that was answered at Dothan. Your line was more with us. What help did you find when you counted again? Day seven hundred thirty-eight.

A renovation is under way. Carpenters, builders and masons are working on the temple in Jerusalem, and the money for timber and hewn stone is being counted out. The king is Josiah. The text says he became king at eight years old, and this is the eighteenth year of his reign. Somewhere in the work, the high priest Hilkiah comes across something and sends word to the king's scribe, Shaphan, in one plain sentence: "I have found the book of the law in the house of the LORD." Found. In the house of the Lord. Where, you'd think, it should never have gone missing. Today is what happens when the king hears it read.
screen: `I HAVE FOUND THE BOOK OF THE LAW.`

segments.voice: Shaphan reads it to himself, then carries it to the king and reads it aloud. And the text says: "when the king had heard the words of the book of the law, that he rent his clothes." Josiah hears words that were in his own temple the whole time, and he tears his clothes. The text never says how the book went missing. No theft, no fire. Some readers picture it lost the quiet way things get lost in a busy house: under other things, while everyone was occupied with the building. Then Josiah does something interesting. He doesn't ask the priests to explain it to him. He sends them to enquire of the Lord, and they go to a prophet, a woman, Huldah, who lives in Jerusalem. Her answer is hard news for the city, but for the king there's a tender line. In the King James Bible, the word to him is: "Because thine heart was tender, and thou hast humbled thyself before the LORD." What saves the moment is not that Josiah already knew. It's that, hearing it late, he let it reach him. And in the next chapter he gathers everyone, small and great, and reads the whole book to them himself. Which book was it? The chapter calls it the book of the law and doesn't say more. Some readers connect it with Deuteronomy. Whatever it was, the story puts the loss somewhere uncomfortable: not out in the world, but inside the house of worship, among people working hard on the building.

Here's the practice: find one book you've lost in the house. Settle, and breathe. Let your mind walk through your rooms, real or not. Is there a book you've let gather dust: a Bible, a letter, a journal, something that once meant a lot? Or a word someone said to you that you've stopped rereading? Don't scold yourself. Josiah wasn't the one who lost it, and he still let it reach him. Just find it, and picture picking it up. If you pray, you can hold it before God for a moment. If you don't, just hold it, and let it be found. The bell holds the time.
Josiah. The young king who heard the book of the law, found in the temple during repairs, and tore his clothes.
Your line: the book was lost in the house. Today, reread one thing you've neglected, even a single page, and let it reach you. Day seven hundred thirty-eight.

739.title: Jerusalem falls (2 Kings 25)
739.hook: the temple burned, the people carried to Babylon
739.carry: even exile is not the end
739.howItsDone: Christians read the fall of Jerusalem and the exile in Bible readings and sermons, sometimes alongside Psalm 137 and the prophets, and some churches pray for refugees and displaced people when these passages come up.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Josiah, told the book of the law was found in the temple during repairs. Your line was the book was lost in the house. What did you pick up and reread? Day seven hundred thirty-nine.
screen: `THE BOOK WAS LOST IN THE HOUSE.`

segments.voice: "By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat down, yea, we wept, when we remembered Zion." That's a psalm, and it's sung by people a very long way from home. How did they get there? The answer is in a hard chapter at the end of Second Kings. An army from Babylon surrounds Jerusalem. The siege goes on until there is no bread left in the city. The wall is broken through. The king, Zedekiah, runs for it by night and is caught near Jericho. And then the Babylonian commander comes to the city with fire. Today's word is what came next for a whole people.

The King James Bible tells it flatly, almost like an inventory: "he burnt the house of the LORD, and the king's house, and all the houses of Jerusalem, and every great man's house burnt he with fire." The temple Solomon prayed in, gone. The walls pulled down. The bronze pillars broken up and carried off as scrap. Then the people. The rest of the city is carried away to Babylon, and the poorest are left behind to tend the vines and the fields. The chapter sums it up in one line: "So Judah was carried away out of their land." That's exile: not just moving, but being taken from the place where your God's house stood, to a city where everything says your story is over. And here's what's worth noticing. The writer of Kings could have stopped there. The burning is the obvious ending. But the chapter keeps going. Years later in Babylon, a new king lets the old exiled king of Judah, Jehoiachin, out of prison. And the text says: "he spake kindly to him." He gives him new clothes instead of prison garments, and a seat at the king's table, every day, for the rest of his life. That's the last scene of the whole book. Not a rescue. Not a return home. Just a man in exile, eating at a table, spoken to kindly. Some readers hear in it a small sign that the line of David isn't finished. Others simply hear that the story kept going. And the psalm from the opening is sung from inside that exile, by the rivers of Babylon. A people who lost their land did not lose their voice.

Here's the practice: remember people far from home. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind people who've lost their homeland: refugees in the news, a family that moved to your street, a coworker who can't go back, maybe your own grandparents. Don't try to solve anything. Picture one face, or one family, at their kitchen table tonight, a long way from where they started. If you pray, you can pray for them in your own words, by name if you know it. If you don't, just hold them in mind for the length of the bell. The bell holds the time.
Exile. Being carried away from your land, as Judah was taken to Babylon when Jerusalem fell and the temple burned.
Your line: even exile is not the end. Today, speak kindly to one person who is far from home, the way a king once did in Babylon. Day seven hundred thirty-nine.

740.title: For such a time (Esther 4:14)
740.hook: a Jewish queen risks her life for her people; Jews keep Purim remembering it
740.carry: for such a time as this
740.howItsDone: Christians read Esther as scripture and sometimes quote Mordecai's for such a time as this when someone takes on a hard calling; Jews keep Purim each year by reading the scroll of Esther aloud, sending food to friends and giving gifts to the poor.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Jerusalem fell and the people went into exile. Your line was even exile is not the end. Who far from home did you speak kindly to? Day seven hundred forty.

The story is set far from Jerusalem, in the Persian royal city of Shushan, among Jews still scattered across the empire. A young Jewish woman, Esther, raised by her cousin Mordecai, has become queen. She has kept quiet about who her people are. Then a powerful official, Haman, angry that Mordecai won't bow to him, gets the king to sign an order to destroy the Jews of the whole empire on a single day. Haman picks the day by casting lots. Mordecai sends word to the palace: go to the king. Esther sends word back: anyone who walks in to the king without being called is put to death, unless he holds out his golden scepter. Mordecai's reply is today.
screen: `GO IN UNCALLED, AND YOU MAY DIE.`

segments.voice: Mordecai doesn't flatter her. He tells her the palace won't hide her, and then, in the King James Bible: "For if thou altogether holdest thy peace at this time, then shall there enlargement and deliverance arise to the Jews from another place." Help will come from somewhere, he says. The only question is whether you'll be part of it. And then the question: "who knoweth whether thou art come to the kingdom for such a time as this?" Who knows. He doesn't claim to be sure. He just asks her to consider that her strange place, a Jewish orphan wearing a Persian crown, might not be an accident. Esther's answer is just as strong. She asks the Jews of the city to fast for her three days, and says she and her maids will fast too. Then: "so will I go in unto the king, which is not according to the law: and if I perish, I perish." She goes in. The king holds out the scepter. And in a complete reversal, Haman ends up on the gallows he built for Mordecai, and the Jews are allowed to defend themselves. The book names the festival that remembers it: "they called these days Purim after the name of Pur," and Pur, the text says, means the lot Haman cast. The book itself asks for days of feasting and joy, sending portions to one another and gifts to the poor, and Jewish tradition keeps Purim by reading the scroll of Esther aloud. Some readers point out that in this book, as the King James Bible prints it, God is never named. And yet Jewish and Christian readers have long heard God at work behind it, through a cousin's question and a queen's nerve.

Here's the practice: find your palace door. Settle, and breathe. Where do you have access that other people don't? A boss who listens to you. A family group chat. A classroom, a committee, a friend who trusts you. Somewhere you could say one true thing that would help someone who can't get in the room. Let one come to mind. Then notice what's keeping you quiet: fear, comfort, not wanting to make it awkward. You don't have to decide anything yet. If you pray, you can bring that door to God. If you don't, just stand in front of it for a while. The bell holds the time.
Purim. The festival named for the lot Haman cast, kept by Jews to remember how Esther went in to the king and her people were saved.
Your line: for such a time as this. Today, speak up once, kindly and clearly, in a place where you have access and someone else doesn't. Day seven hundred forty.

741.title: Weeping and shouting (Ezra 3:10–13)
741.hook: the temple foundation is laid; the young shout, the old weep, and no one can tell the sounds apart
741.howItsDone: Christians sometimes read Ezra 3 at the dedication of a new church building or at moments of new beginning after loss, and some churches mark such days with both thanksgiving and remembrance.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Esther went in to the king uncalled, and Jews keep Purim to remember it. Your line was for such a time as this. Where did you speak up? Day seven hundred forty-one.

Two days ago the temple burned. Today, in the story, the people are back. The book of Ezra opens with a Persian king, Cyrus, giving the exiles leave to go home to Jerusalem and build the house of the Lord again. Some go. Where the temple stood, they set up the altar first, on its old bases, and then, with stonecutters and carpenters and cedar wood brought by sea, they start on the foundation. And on the day the foundation is laid, the priests stand in their robes with trumpets, the Levites with cymbals, and they sing together by turns. Then something happens that the writer can't quite describe without a strange sentence. That sentence is today.

The song they sing is short. They praise the Lord, the King James Bible says, "because he is good, for his mercy endureth for ever toward Israel." And the people shout with a great shout, because the foundation is laid. But not everyone shouts. "Many of the priests and Levites and chief of the fathers, who were ancient men, that had seen the first house, when the foundation of this house was laid before their eyes, wept with a loud voice." The old ones remember. They had seen the first house. And what they see now is a foundation, a beginning, and maybe a smaller one. So they weep, loudly, at the same moment many others are shouting for joy. Then the strange sentence: "So that the people could not discern the noise of the shout of joy from the noise of the weeping of the people: for the people shouted with a loud shout, and the noise was heard afar off." From far enough away, you'd hear one sound. You couldn't tell which part was grief and which was joy. The writer doesn't correct either group. Nobody tells the old men to cheer up, and nobody tells the young ones to be quiet out of respect. Both sounds belong to the day. Both are true. Something precious was lost, and something real is beginning, and the text lets them rise together. Some readers think of this scene at weddings after a death in the family, at a new church building where the old one stood, at a graduation a grandparent didn't live to see. One sound, heard afar off.

Here's the practice: hold both at once. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind something in your life right now that's mixed: a move, a new job, a child leaving home, a recovery, a change that's good and still costs something. Let the joyful part come up. Don't push the grief away when it comes too. Let them sit side by side, the way the shout and the weeping did, without deciding which one wins. If you pray, you can bring both to God together. If you don't, just let your breath carry both. The bell holds the time.
Cyrus. The Persian king who let the exiles go home, where the old wept and the young shouted for joy as the new temple's foundation was laid.
Your line: joy and grief, one sound. Today, when someone's happy news carries a loss inside it, make room for both when you answer them. Day seven hundred forty-one.

what a scholar hears: Ezra 3:13 says the people could not discern the shout of joy from the weeping, and the whole noise was heard afar off.

742.title: Nehemiah's wall (Nehemiah 2–4)
742.hook: a cupbearer weeps, prays, and rebuilds with a trowel in one hand and a sword in the other
742.carry: let us rise up and build
742.howItsDone: Christians sometimes read Nehemiah when a church or community starts a building or repair project, and some take up his quick prayer between two sentences as a model for praying in the middle of a hard conversation.

segments.voice: Yesterday, foundation day under Cyrus, when the old wept and the young shouted. Your line was joy and grief, one sound. Where did you hear both at once? Day seven hundred forty-two.

Nehemiah has a good job. He's cupbearer to the king of Persia, the man who hands the king his wine. Then visitors arrive from Judah, and he asks how Jerusalem is doing. Badly, they say. The wall is broken down and the gates are burned. Nehemiah writes: "I sat down and wept, and mourned certain days, and fasted, and prayed before the God of heaven." Later he's serving wine, and the king notices his face. Why is your face sad, when you're not sick? Nehemiah is frightened. He's about to ask the king for something enormous. And between the king's question and his answer, there's one half-line that's today.

The king asks, what do you want? And Nehemiah writes: "So I prayed to the God of heaven." That's it. No time for a long prayer. A breath of a prayer between a question and an answer, standing beside the throne with the wine. Then he asks: send me to rebuild the city. And the king says yes. In Jerusalem, Nehemiah doesn't start with a speech. He goes out at night, quietly, with a few men, and rides around the ruins to see the damage for himself. Only then does he gather the people and tell them what he saw and how God had helped him. Their answer: "Let us rise up and build. So they strengthened their hands for this good work." Chapter three is a long list of names and gates: who repaired which stretch, families, priests, goldsmiths, apothecaries, some working on the section by their own house. Then the mocking starts. Sanballat and Tobiah, local officials who oppose the work, laugh at it. Tobiah's joke is in the text: "even that which they build, if a fox go up, he shall even break down their stone wall." Then the mocking turns into threats of attack. So Nehemiah sets guards, and the builders change how they work. "Every one with one of his hands wrought in the work, and with the other hand held a weapon." A trowel in one hand, a sword at the side. They kept building anyway. Some Christians read this as a picture of steady work under pressure: you pray in a breath, you look at the damage honestly, you build your own stretch, and you don't stop because someone is laughing.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: walk around one broken wall. Settle, and breathe. Like Nehemiah riding out at night, look honestly at one thing in your life that's broken: a friendship, a habit, a room, a promise you didn't keep. Don't fix it yet. Just see the damage clearly, without blaming anyone. Then find one stretch, the small section by your own house, that you could repair. If you pray, you can do what Nehemiah did between two sentences and pray to the God of heaven. If you don't, just name the stretch. The bell holds the time.
Nehemiah's wall. Jerusalem's broken wall, rebuilt by builders each working their own stretch, with one hand on the work and the other on a weapon.
